stances.claim: The CPRA marks its third anniversary this month -- since its May 30 2023 effectivity, the SC has decided about 100 cases enforcing its provisions, with ~80 ending in disciplinary sanctions and ~20 in dismissals, judicial clemency, or denial of requests.

The Court adopted the CPRA to keep up with changing times and 'recent developments and technological trends which impact the experience and behavior of members of the Philippine Bar, mostly through social media and the internet' -- reasserting its constitutional authority (Section 5[5], Article VIII) to regulate both admission to the practice of law and the behavior and ethical conduct of lawyers.
stances.confidence: asserted with verbatim self-quotation from SC adoption rationale

stances.claim: Six CPRA canons must guide the ethical compass of every lawyer -- Independence (I), Propriety (II), Fidelity (III), Competence and Diligence (IV), Equality (V), Accountability (VI) -- back-referenced to CJP's Dec 4 2023 'Duties of lawyers' column.

Today's focus: decisions meting out penalties -- disbarment, suspension, revocation of notarial commissions, disqualification as notary public, fines, or combinations depending on misconduct gravity. Examples: (1) lawyer suspended five years for client-trust violation via repeated court absences + noncompliance + dereliction under Canon IV; (2) high government official fined for indirect contempt + 'Grossly Undignified Conduct Prejudicial to the Administration of Justice' under Canon VI for publicly assailing conflict-of-interest rule + office order 'effectively encouraged disobedience' violating Canons II and III; (3) prominent practicing lawyer/academic fined P100,000 for simple misconduct under Canon II for sponsoring IBP officer travel -- 'crossed the borders on excessive ... propriety.'

The supreme penalty of disbarment is imposed for 'any misconduct, whether in his [or her] professional or private capacity, which shows him [or her] to be wanting in moral character, in honesty, probity, and good demeanor, or unworthy to continue as an officer of the court.' Novel CPRA Sections 36 to 44 of Canon II require responsible use of social media -- attorneys must 'uphold the dignity of the legal profession in all social media interactions.' Thus the Court condemned a lawyer for indirect contempt after a now-deleted Facebook post accusing the Court of judicial tyranny -- baseless accusations subjecting the tribunal to public ridicule and mockery.

The SC has zero tolerance for dishonesty -- a lawyer who submitted pleadings bearing a fake MCLE number was disbarred for 'patently false information in pleadings ... bad faith and dishonesty ... blatant disrespect of the court and its rules.' Lawyers are expected to protect clients' causes with utmost diligence -- yet some members have treated these obligations with alarming casualness: one disbarred for misappropriating over P60 million from clients (Canon III violation); another disbarred for habitually missing hearings, resulting in the waiver of his client's right to cross-examine a witness and ultimately the imposition of two counts of frustrated homicide (Canons III and IV).

The power to disbar 'must be exercised with great caution,' and the Court's disciplinary authority covers only acts that may affect public confidence and does not extend to enforcing private rights unrelated to a lawyer's duties. The intensified CPRA enforcement should not be mistaken as a campaign of fear -- it is a determined effort to uphold and preserve society's last bulwark of justice and democratic order.

notable_anecdotes: The 'crossed the borders on excessive ... propriety' verbatim citation against the prominent practicing lawyer/academic who sponsored IBP officers' travel -- a striking ethics-line-drawing instance involving an unnamed but presumably well-known figure who compromised IBP's integrity/impartiality/independence.

The high-government-official fined for indirect contempt and 'Grossly Undignified Conduct' for publicly assailing the conflict-of-interest rule and issuing an office order that 'effectively encouraged disobedience' -- among the most striking CPRA Canon VI enforcement instances against a sitting executive-branch official.
The now-deleted Facebook post accusing the SC of 'judicial tyranny' triggering indirect contempt -- captures CPRA's social-media-era teeth in real-world application.
The P60 million misappropriation disbarment -- the magnitude alone signals the scale of client-trust violations CPRA Canon III is meant to deter.

The two-counts-of-frustrated-homicide outcome from a lawyer's habitual hearing-misses -- a vivid worst-case Canon III/IV violation where attorney dereliction directly resulted in client criminal conviction.
The fake-MCLE-number disbarment -- a clean illustration of CPRA's 'zero tolerance for dishonesty' principle.

The 'society's last bulwark of justice and democratic order' closing -- a register-elevated closing-phrase elevating CPRA enforcement from bar-discipline housekeeping to constitutional-stewardship narrative.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the third anniversary of the lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA) -- effective May 30 2023 -- by surveying the SC's enforcement record: about 100 cases decided, ~80 ending in disciplinary sanctions, ~20 in dismissals/judicial clemency/denial of requests. The CPRA replaced the circa-1988 Code of Professional Responsibility to keep up with 'recent developments and technological trends which impact the experience and behavior of members of the Philippine Bar, mostly through social media and the internet,' with the Court reasserting its constitutional authority (Section 5[5], Article VIII) to regulate both admission to the practice of law and the behavior and ethical conduct of lawyers. CJP's Dec 4 2023 'Duties of lawyers' column discussed the six CPRA canons that must guide every lawyer's ethical compass: Independence (I), Propriety (II), Fidelity (III), Competence and Diligence (IV), Equality (V), and Accountability (VI). Today's focus is on penalty-imposing decisions: disbarment, suspension, revocation of notarial commissions, disqualification as notary public, fines, or combinations depending on misconduct gravity. Recent illustrations: (1) a lawyer suspended five years for client-trust violation via repeated court absences + noncompliance + dereliction under Canon IV; (2) a high government official fined for indirect contempt + 'Grossly Undignified Conduct Prejudicial to the Administration of Justice' under Canon VI for publicly assailing the Court's conflict-of-interest rule and issuing an office order that 'effectively encouraged disobedience' violating Canons II and III; (3) a prominent practicing lawyer and academic fined P100,000 for simple misconduct under Canon II for sponsoring IBP officers' travel -- 'crossed the borders on excessive ... propriety' compromising IBP integrity. Disbarment is imposed for 'any misconduct, whether in his [or her] professional or private capacity, which shows him [or her] to be wanting in moral character, in honesty, probity, and good demeanor, or unworthy to continue as an officer of the court.' Novel CPRA Sections 36 to 44 of Canon II require responsible social-media use -- attorneys must 'uphold the dignity of the legal profession in all social media interactions.' Thus the Court condemned a lawyer for indirect contempt after a now-deleted Facebook post accusing the Court of judicial tyranny -- baseless accusations subjecting the tribunal to ridicule. The SC has zero tolerance for dishonesty: a lawyer who submitted pleadings bearing a fake Mandatory Continuing Legal Education number was disbarred for 'patently false information ... bad faith and dishonesty ... blatant disrespect.' One lawyer was disbarred for misappropriating over P60 million entrusted by clients (Canon III); another was disbarred for habitually missing hearings, resulting in the waiver of his client's cross-examination right and the imposition of two counts of frustrated homicide (Canons III + IV). The Court is mindful, however, that disbarment 'must be exercised with great caution,' and its disciplinary authority covers only acts affecting public confidence and does not extend to enforcing private rights unrelated to a lawyer's duties. The high tribunal's intensified CPRA enforcement should not be mistaken as a campaign of fear -- it is a determined effort to uphold and preserve society's last bulwark of justice and democratic order.
